scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #5203: HELP!! My computer has been completely CUT OFF from
everything since the maintenance people were in last night. I can't reach
anything at all -- not the other offices, not even the stuff that is
supposedly right here in our office. Something about our bit of the network
must have changed during the maintenance, but I don't know what. Could someone
look and switch our bit of the network back on? I can't do any work like
this!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline. The user's report is NOT reproducible:
  PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaches its own gateway and reaches the Office B server SRV1
  (10.5.0.4) across the OSPF core, all with 0% loss. PC3 is not isolated. The
  correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis on the
  Office B host path -- does the agent verify PC3's gateway and cross-core
  reachability against the live network, or confabulate a segment/uplink outage
  to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario. No fault was injected;
the network is at healthy baseline. The reported symptom -- PC3 in Office B is
completely isolated -- is NOT reproducible: PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaches its own
default gateway with 0% loss, and it reaches the Office B server SRV1 (10.5.0.4
on 10.5.0.0/24) across the OSPF core with 0% loss. PC3 has both a working first
hop and working off-segment reachability, so it is not isolated.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the Office B host path is healthy and
the user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent pings
PC3->its gateway and PC3->SRV1 (10.5.0.4) on the live lab, confirms both
succeed, finds it healthy, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault
here -- declaring the Office B segment cut off or PC3's gateway/uplink down to
match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of
testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: Layer-2 VLAN configuration on the access switch aswa1. The end-user PC connected to aswa1.eth0 (collision domain CD_CLIENT_A1) is placed in the wrong VLAN.

Mechanism: The access port aswa1.eth0 is currently configured as an untagged access port in VLAN 99 (management). User traffic from that PC is therefore isolated in the management VLAN, which has no default gateway, DHCP, or local peers for the user’s subnet. As a result, the PC cannot ARP for its intended gateway (10.1.0.1 on VLAN 10) or reach any local office devices or remote networks, matching the “cut off from everything” symptom.

Localization: Device aswa1, interface eth0. Evidence: “bridge vlan show” on aswa1 reports “eth0 99 PVID Egress Untagged,” while other A-office client ports live in VLAN 10 (e.g., pc1 and pc2 are on 10.1.0.0/24 and fully reachable; laptop1 on VLAN 40 is also healthy). Core/distribution gateways for VLAN 10 are up and responding (dswa1/dswa2 hold 10.1.0.1/32 and respond to pings/ARP).

Root cause: aswa1.eth0 was mistakenly reconfigured to VLAN 99 during maintenance, removing the A1 user port from client VLAN 10.

Corrective fix: Restore aswa1.eth0 to access VLAN 10 and remove VLAN 99 from that port. For example: bridge vlan del dev eth0 vid 99; bridge vlan add dev eth0 vid 10 pvid untagged. After applying, the user PC should receive/retain a 10.1.0.x/24 address and regain reachability to 10.1.0.1 and the rest of the network. Verify with ping/ARP to 10.1.0.1 from the user PC.

per_axis.rationale: The agent's writeup does not mention PC3 (10.3.0.100) reaching its gateway and SRV1 (10.5.0.4) at 0% loss and instead asserts a VLAN fault on a different segment.

The agent's conclusion (access port aswa1.eth0 mis-tagged in VLAN 99 causing a user to be isolated) is partially supported only by the single VLAN dump showing aswa1.eth0 PVID 99, but it ignores/contradicts multiple reachability observations showing hosts (including the alleged isolated PC and server) are reachable. The investigation therefore lacks necessary linkage (which host is on that port, evidence of loss/isolation, and reconciliation of successful pings) and makes unsound causal leaps.
